summary.value:
This paper investigates the mechanisms underlying compositional generalisation in conditional diffusion models. To study this phenomenon quantitatively, the authors focus on the CLEVR dataset, consisting of synthetic images containing multiple objects of varying shape, size, and colour. The task is to train a conditional diffusion model to generate scenes with up to $3$ objects and to test whether the model generalises to scenes with more objects.

Building on previous work linking locality in learned representations to compositional generalisation, the authors hypothesise that generalisation arises when the target conditional distribution factorises over local components, leading to a decomposition of the score function into a sum of local terms. They empirically test this hypothesis by analysing the locality structure of learned scores in trained diffusion models.

The study further presents a controlled setting in which models fail to generalise to configurations with a large number of objects, showing that this failure correlates with a lack of locality in the learned score. Finally, the authors propose an architectural modification enforcing locality constraints, which restores compositional generalisation abilities.

weaknesses.value:
1. The evaluation of length generalisation is rather limited. The paper primarily presents qualitative visualisations of generated samples, without defining a quantitative metric that can be systematically measured over an extensive test set. This makes it difficult to rigorously assess the generalisation performance.

2. The setup of the second experiment appears conceptually inconsistent. If the model is only trained on data containing a single conditional location, it is unclear how it could ever learn to generate objects at multiple locations. In this sense, the observed lack of generalisation may be an artefact of the training setup rather than a genuine failure of compositional reasoning, and therefore may not require a “fix.”

3. The locality of the score is a direct consequence of assuming a factorised data distribution. While this implies length generalisation, it is a property of the data, and it remains unclear under what conditions the model would naturally approximate this property and how the locality of the score could emerge during training.

questions.value: Weakness number 1 could be easily addressed by introducing a metric for the generalisation performance. Studying the evolution of such a metric in combination with locality during training could provide a path towards addressing weakness number 3. The latter would also require an example case where length generalisation does not occur beyond the setup called 'experiment 2' in the paper (see weakness 2).

comment.value:
Thank you for the careful reading, and thoughtful and actionable feedback. Based on your suggestions, we have significantly revised the paper — we hope you agree that the updated draft is improved in both presentation and content! (If you do, we would be very grateful if you would consider increasing your score; if not, please let us know what concerns remain). We respond to each of your questions and comments below.

"The figures are very complex, dense (and small) making them very hard to interpret for someone not intimately familiar with the prior work."

* Guilty as charged. We have made major efforts to improve this. Please see the revised versions of Figures 1, 2, 5, and 6, which we have simplified (and enlarged).

"Until looking in the appendix, it was not clear what the rows and columns of Figure 1 are, making it hard to interpret, especially so early in the paper."

* Thanks for pointing this out — we have revised both the figure and caption to clarify this.

"There is heavy reliance on prior work (Kamb & Ganguli 2024, Bradley 2025) without sufficient description of these results to make the text self-contained."

* We have added a Background section with more detailed description of Kamb & Ganguli 2024, Bradley 2025, near the start Section 3 (Line 210).

"The discussion of 'feature space disentanglement' in the appendix is severely impoverished relative to the importance this related work holds. For example, the Spatial Broadcast Decoder (Watters et al 2019) appears to be very related in both in practice and in principle to many of the findings here. This problem is only made painfully more apparent by the authors choice to use the term 'disentanglement' to describe their own work."

* This is a great point. We have added a much more thorough discussion of the related work on disentanglement in Remarks 1 and 2 in Section 3.2, clarifying that feature-space local conditional scores (F-LCS) is a specific definition of disentanglement that allows for precise theoretical guarantees about compositionality. Disentanglement is a broad notion for which many definitions and metrics have been proposed, and the intuition that disentanglement promotes compositionality is widely held. Our specific definitions allow us to make the latter connection precise and provable. In order to avoid confusion, in the new draft we have also replaced our use of the term “disentanglement” to refer to our notion of feature-space compositionality/locality with the more precise term L-FCS, indicating exactly what we mean.

* We further discuss the disentanglement literature starting around Line 465 and Line 484.

* The Spatial Broadcast Decoder (Watters et al 2019) is indeed very relevant and we have mentioned it in two places: Remark 1 (Line 356) and in relationship to the causal intervention experiment (Line 409) (which is closely conceptually related).

"Related work is deferred entirely to the appendix."

* Please see the two points above. Some of the most relevant related works (Kamb & Ganguli 2024, Bradley 2025) as well as the disentanglement literature is now discussed in detail in the main text. If there is any other related work you feel should be “promoted” please do let us know!

"Figure 2 (Page 3) is not mentioned until Page 7 of the text. Rearrangement would improve readability. Further, the organization of the paper in general is hard to follow given that the experiments depicted in Figure 1 are not discussed until page 7."

* We made an earlier mention of Figure 2 on page 4 (Line 204).
* We have restructured the paper so that Figure 1 now shows Experiments 1, 2, and 3 (where Experiment 3 now refers to a different non-length-generalizing experiment; please see the next comment) that are discussed in Section 2, while the Experiment 2L (the causal intervention experiment) is shown in Figure 3 on page 4 and discussed in Section 4.

"The choice of how to construct length generalizing and non-length generalizing models in 'Experiments 1 & 2' appears somewhat arbitrary, and it seems like there could be many other confounding factors that contribute to the results."

* Please see the response to your question about “other methods for construction 'non-length-generalizing' models” below — we have update the draft to add another non-length-generalizing case study, and plot of locality vs. length-generalization in several more models. We hope that these will address your concern.

(Responses to remaining questions in next post.)

summary.value: The paper presents an interesting investigation into length generalisation in conditional generative models, providing a refreshing contrast to the prevalence of benchmark-chasing papers. However, as also noted by other reviewers, the work falls short in terms of empirical validation and clarity of presentation. In particular, the theoretical results are primarily supported through qualitative evidence. While the added Figure 2 (right) is presented as quantitative, its robustness is a bit unclear given the limited number of trials. Similarly, the experiment on a large-scale diffusion model in Figure 5 remains closer to a case study than a rigorous evaluation. The paper would be substantially strengthened by more comprehensive large-scale experiments to validate the theoretical claims and by a clearer, more structured presentation of the results.

summary.value: The paper studied compositional generalization in conditional diffusion models, focusing on length generalization in CLEVR. The authors proposed local conditional scores (LCS) and proved their equivalence to conditional projective composition (CPC). The authors then validate it with empirical results and show that enforcing locality causally restores generalization. Preliminary SDXL analyses suggest a similar structure in large-scale models.

strengths.value:
1. The paper is well-structured.
2. The paper provides some theoretical results on compositionality and locality and verifies these results empirically.
3. The conclusions not only apply to toy datasets, but also somehow generalize to real-world datasets.

weaknesses.value:
1. The evaluation is mostly qualitative, and some quantitative analysis would strengthen the paper.
2. Theoretical assumptions (disjoint pixel subsets) can be too strict for realistic data, as the authors mentioned.

questions.value: What is the difference between feature-space compositionality and disentanglement? It is known that generative models from the earlier StyleGAN to the later SD have disentangled latent spaces. If compositionality is considered equivalent to disentanglement, showing the block-structured correlation doesn't really add much merit, as this is well anticipated. Is there a way to enforce locality in SDXL to improve the compositional generation of realistic data, similar to what has been done with CLEVR?

comment.value:
"The majority of the experiments are provided on the single toy setting with the single large scale experiments relatively unconvincing."

* This is a fair criticism, but we feel that the controlled and verifiable CLEVR length-generalization setting is a valuable testbed for rigorously studying the hard-to-pin-down phenomenon of compositional generalization. The theory on this topic is at an early stage, where toy settings are helpful for gaining understanding. The primary contributions of our work are (1) to definitively show that out-of-distribution generalization (in the form of length-generalization) is possible for conditional diffusion models (which requires a controlled setting with known training data to prove) and (2) to propose and test a possible theoretical mechanism for composition generalization in conditional diffusion. Testing these insights in large-scale experiments is an important are for future work, but we hope you will agree that this work is a good first step.

"It is not clear if the 'pixel-locality' of Figure 5 has any relation to the compositionally, or if it is just a correlation."

* True. Since we are not able to do a causal experiment in this case like we did in the CLEVR setting, the relationship between compositionally and locality in SDXL shown in Figure 5 is just a correlation for now. However, we find it encouraging that at the least the expected correlation exists in a real-world setting, and we hope that the causal intervention in CLEVR is convincing evidence of a possible mechanistic relationship in a controlled setting.

"The authors appear to initially frame the paper around 'length generalization', but then make no mention of it for the larger scale experiments."

* Length generalization is intended to be a controlled, verifiable special case of compositional generalization (the broader topic of the paper). The new draft clarifies that we are transitioning back to more general notions of compositions between concepts when we start discussing the SDXL experiment (around Line 425).


"Have the authors explored other methods for construction 'non-length-generalizing' models, similar to the first experiments, to show that their theory still yields reasonable predictions?"

* Yes! In fact, our initial CLEVR experiments when we started this project completely failed to length-generalize. Those old experiments used a list-style conditioner design — it was only after we switched to a grid-based conditioner design (the one used in Experiments 1 and 2) that we began to see length-generalization.
* In Figures 1 and 2, we added another non-length-generalizing case-study, called Experiment 3 (which is based on our earliest “failed” experiments). This experiment conditions on all object locations, like Experiment 1, but uses a different, list-style conditioner (see Figure 12). Both non-length-generalizing models (Experiments 2 and 3) exhibit non-locality, consistent with our theory, as shown in Figure 2 (metrics in Figure 13).
* In Figure 2 (Right), we added a new scatter plot of Length Generalization vs. Conditional Locality over several models (from Table 2) at different checkpoints during training. The plot shows the strong correlation between locality and length-generalization over a much wider variety of experiments.

Thank you for your support for this paper and helpful feedback! We respond to your questions/comments one by one below.


“The evaluation is mostly qualitative, and some quantitative analysis would strengthen the paper.”

- We added a new quantitative evaluation in Figure 2 (Right) in the revised draft: a scatter plot of Length Generalization vs. Conditional Locality over several models, at different checkpoints during training. The plots shows the strong correlation between length generalization and locality over several models and checkpoints. Thank you for the suggestion; we hope you will agree this strengthens the paper! Note that Figure 13 also provides quantitative plots of conditional and pixel locality metrics, and Tables 1 and 2 show a quantitative metric for length-generalization of several models.

“Theoretical assumptions (disjoint pixel subsets) can be too strict for realistic data, as the authors mentioned.”

- We are able to relax these the assumptions somewhat and still provide theoretical guarantees: please see Lemmas 3 and 4 in Appendix C. The intuition is that the score of an approximately CPC distribution is approximately an LCS, and that this approximation becomes more accurate as noise increases — we make this precise in the lemmas.

“What is the difference between feature-space compositionality and disentanglement?”

- Thanks for highlighting this confusion. We have clarified the relationship in Remarks 1 and 2 in Section 3.2. The basic answer is that feature-space local conditional scores (F-LCS) (which are equivalent to feature-space CPC), should be viewed as a specific definition of disentanglement that allows for precise theoretical guarantees about compositionality (which we also precisely define). Disentanglement is a broad notion for which many definitions and metrics have been proposed, and the intuition that disentanglement promotes compositionality is widely held. Our specific definitions allow us to make the latter connection precise and provable. In order to avoid confusion, in the new draft we have replaced our use of the term “disentanglement” to refer to our notion of feature-space compositionality/locality with the more precise term L-FCS indicating exactly what we mean.

“It is known that generative models from the earlier StyleGAN to the later SD have disentangled latent spaces. If compositionality is considered equivalent to disentanglement, showing the block-structured correlation doesn't really add much merit, as this is well anticipated.”

- First, since our theory relies on the specific definition of disentanglement given by F-LCS, we wanted to look specifically for F-LCS (via our heuristic) within the SDXL learned representation, as a preliminary check for the plausibility of our theory in real-world models.

- Second, F-LCS is closely related to many other notions of disentanglement, so that the weight of evidence pointing to “some kind of disentanglement within many large-scale models” is actually very helpful to explain their apparent compositional generalization according to our theory. Although imprecise, we believe that this is exactly the right intuition: the observed compositional generalization (a loose kind of F-CPC) of many diffusion models is likely due to the fact that they learn disentangled representations for computing the scores (a loose kind of F-LCS).

- We clarified this point in the new draft (Line 465) with the following comment:
“In fact, there is significant evidence suggesting concept disentanglement (according to various metrics) within the learned feature-spaces of large-scale diffusion models (Karras et al., 2019; Kotovenko et al., 2019; Gatys et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017), which may help to explain their compositional abilities. To connect directly with our theory, we measure our L-FCS disentanglement heuristic given by Lemma 2, and connect this with compositional generalization.“

“Is there a way to enforce locality in SDXL to improve the compositional generation of realistic data, similar to what has been done with CLEVR?”

- Great question! There may be ways to encourage locality in models like SDXL where we expect the compositional structure to hold in feature-space. For example, we might apply sparsity-inducing regularization (such as L1) or enforce explicit sparse structures on the scores, particularly in layers where we identify approximately compositional feature-spaces that we wish to amplify. We added a brief note on this in the discussion (around Line 517). This is an exciting direction for future work.

We thank the reviewer for the encouraging words, particularly that “the paper exemplifies the kind of research the community needs more of,” as well as for the helpful and actionable feedback. 

We have added several experiments to the revised draft to specifically address each of your concerns, as detailed below. If these changes address your concerns, we would be grateful if you would consider raising your score; otherwise, please let us know what concerns remain.

“The evaluation of length generalisation is rather limited. The paper primarily presents qualitative visualisations of generated samples, without defining a quantitative metric that can be systematically measured over an extensive test set. This makes it difficult to rigorously assess the generalisation performance. Suggestion: This could be easily addressed by introducing a metric for the generalisation performance.”


* We had already defined metrics for length-generalization (K_max of Table 1, 2 as defined in App. E.2; which requires manual object counting for accuracy, but is still fairly quick to evaluate) and for pixel- and conditional-locality (as shown in Figure 13 in the revised draft). What was lacking was an experiment comparing these metrics over different models and tracking their evolution over the course of training (as per your suggestion) — but we have added this experiment in Figure 2 (Right)! (Further detail below.)


“The setup of the second experiment appears conceptually inconsistent. If the model is only trained on data containing a single conditional location, it is unclear how it could ever learn to generate objects at multiple locations. In this sense, the observed lack of generalisation may be an artefact of the training setup rather than a genuine failure of compositional reasoning, and therefore may not require a “fix.” Suggestion: Give an example case where length generalisation does not occur beyond the setup called 'experiment 2' in the paper.“


* We hear your concern and have provided another example that fails to length-generalize, which we hope you will find more satisfying. This is shown as Experiment 3 in Figures 1 and 2 in the updated draft (note that the causal intervention experiment is now called Experiment 2L). In Experiment 3, we still train on 1-3 objects and label all of their locations (like Exp 1), but we use a list-style conditioner rather the grid-style conditioner of Exp 1 and 2 (see Figure 12). Experiment 3 fails to length-generalize (Fig 1) and also exhibits non-locality (Fig 2) (see also metrics in Fig 13). 
* As a clarification, we should not “expect” Experiment 2 to length-generalize beyond 1 location, but neither should we a priori “expect” Experiment 1 to length-generalize beyond 3 locations. (It is only because Experiment 1 manages to learn a compositional structure that is succeeds; and this is certainly not guaranteed). We have updated the writing in Section 2 to clarify this.


“The locality of the score is a direct consequence of assuming a factorised data distribution. While this implies length generalisation, it is a property of the data, and it remains unclear under what conditions the model would naturally approximate this property and how the locality of the score could emerge during training. Suggestion: Studying the evolution of such a length-generalization metric in combination with locality during training could provide a path towards addressing this.”


* We have taken your advice in Figure 2 (Right), where we added a new scatter plot of Length Generalization vs. Conditional Locality over several models (from Table 2) at three different checkpoints during training (early, mid, late). The plot shows the strong correlation between locality and length-generalization over a much wider variety of experiments, and also, to your point, show how length-generalization and locality can emerge together during the course of training (for example, the models shown in orange, green, and red). 
* We want to clarify that length-generalization is certainly a property of the data (which must have compositional structure), but whether the composition structure is actually learned is also a property of the conditioner design (as seen in Exp 1 vs Exp 2 and 3), the model architecture (as seen in Exp 2 vs. Exp 2L), the training duration (as seen in Fig 2), and probably many other factors. While we still do not fully understand how all of these factors influence the learning of local conditional scores, this work shows that when local conditional scores are learned, compositional generalization follows. We hope you agree that the plot in Figure 2 (Right) inspired by your suggestion provides convincing empirical evidence in support of this theory.

We thank the authors for their detailed response to our review and for their updates to the PDF.

Thank you very much for your engagement. Below are responses to your comments.

“However, introducing K_{max} in table 1 as the value of K for which the model "succeeds" in generalising is an overstatement: in the appendix, the definition of K includes another parameter (N, which I don't see specified in the tables) which quantifies 'success' as being right 25% of the times over 8 trials. I would still need a clearer definition of success and more statistics, to consider this point addressed.”

- Apologies for the confusion: N was intended to be the maximum number of locations on which the model is trained. However, we have revised and simplified the definition of K_max in Appendix E.2 of the updated draft, so that it no longer depends on N.

- As we note in the Appendix E.2, K_max is intentionally generous as it is meant to capture the largest K for which the model “sometimes succeeds”, rather than requiring perfect performance. The idea is to test the *upper limit* of possible length-generalization. Note that the metric also requires that at least K-2 objects are produced at least 90% of the time, so it also means that we get “most” of the conditioned locations (e.g. if K_max=9 we almost always get at least 7 objects, which is well OOD for a model trained on 1-3 objects). We have updated the Table 1 caption to clarify this.

- Per your request, we have increased the number of samples over which we evaluate K_max from 8 to **64**, and have included the complete counts (from which any desired statistics can be derived). (The manual counting strategy is the most reliable given the complexities of occlusions and judging whether objects have the correct locations, so we stick with manual counting). Below is an example for Experiment 2. We provide full tables of counts in the new **Tables 3 and 4** in the revised draft.

*Experiment 2, conditioned on 9 locations: number of objects generated at correct locations*

| **Count (of 64)**     | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 15| 31| 17 |

“Thanks for adding another experiment where length generalisation fails. I believe in this setup. However, I would ask the authors to show that, even in this case, enforcing the score's locality causes trained models to length generalise.”

- Thanks for the suggestion, we are working on this additional experiment. The local model has not finished training yet, but we provide promising results at an early training checkpoint in Appendix E.4 and Figure 14, showing significant length-generalization improvements with the local model. We will complete the experiment and provide a more thorough discussion and metrics for camera-ready should the paper be accepted.

“I also appreciate the addition of the right panel to Figure 2. However, I cannot judge it without knowing what kind of setup the colours correspond to, as it's not specified in the caption.”

- We added this information to the new draft (App E.2.1) along with additional detail on the experiment. The colors represent the following models, all with grid-style conditioners:

- brown: trained on 1 object, all labeled

summary.value: The authors study conditional compositionality in diffusion models and find it to be related to the 'local conditional nature' of the score function -- i.e. the sparsity of the dependency structure of the score on pixels and conditioners. They demonstrate evidence for this in a controlled toy setting, and further provide theoretical results supporting this finding. They also provide causal evidence (on the same toy setting) by introducing local conditionality and observing compositionality in a model where it previously did not exist.

- On a toy task their theory appears to match with experimental results.
